Barely means only just — something is true, but only to the smallest possible degree. It sits right at the edge, almost at zero, but not quite.

Think of a line. On one end is "completely," on the other end is "not at all." Barely lives right next to "not at all" — but it is still on the yes side of the line.

"He barely passed the exam."

He passed. But only just. One mark more and it would have been a fail.
The Most Important Thing to Understand: "Barely" vs. "Almost"

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

  • Barely = it happened, but only just.
  • Almost = it did not happen, but it came close.

"She barely finished the race." → She finished. (But it was very hard, and she almost didn't.)
"She almost finished the race." → She did NOT finish. (But she came close.)

Same situation, completely different outcomes. "Barely" confirms the event happened. "Almost" says it didn't.

1. A very small amount — almost nothing

You use "barely" when there is so little of something that it almost doesn't count.

"There was barely enough food for two people."

(There was food, but it was the minimum — any less and it wouldn't have been enough.)

"I barely slept last night."

(I slept, but only a tiny amount — maybe one or two hours.)

"There was barely a drop of water left in the bottle."

(Almost empty, but not completely.)

2. Great difficulty — almost impossible

When someone can do something, but only with extreme effort, you say they "can barely" do it.

"After the accident, he could barely walk."

(He walked, but with enormous difficulty. Every step was a struggle.)

"I was so tired I could barely keep my eyes open."

(My eyes were open, but only just — they kept trying to close.)

"She spoke so softly that I could barely hear her."

(I heard her, but only just — any softer and I wouldn't have heard a word.)

3. A very short time ago — almost immediately

"Barely" is also used when one event happens immediately after another, with almost no time in between. This often uses the pattern "had barely... when..."

"We had barely sat down when the waiter came."

(We sat down, and almost instantly — before we even settled — the waiter appeared.)

"She had barely stepped outside when it began to rain."

(The moment she stepped out — almost before she could react — rain started.)

"He had barely finished speaking when the audience began to applaud."

The feeling here is: so soon! There was almost no gap at all.

4. A very small age, size, or measure

"Barely" is used to say something is just above a number — almost below it.

"The child was barely three years old."

(Just turned three, or close to it — very young.)

"The shelf was barely wide enough to hold the books."

(It fit — but only just. A centimetre less and it wouldn't have.)

"He is barely five feet tall."

(He is five feet, but only just — very close to being under five feet.)

The word often brings an emotional shade to the sentence:

  • Relief: "We barely caught the train." (Phew! We made it, but it was so close.)
  • Struggle or difficulty: "I could barely breathe in that heat."
  • Surprise: "He had barely arrived when he had to leave again." (So fast!)
  • Inadequacy: "There was barely enough money to pay the rent." (Not really comfortable — just the minimum.)
"Barely" and Negative Words — An Important Grammar Rule

Because "barely" already carries a near-negative meaning (almost nothing, almost not), you must never combine it with another negative word like "not," "never," or "no."

❌ "I can't barely see anything." — This is wrong (double negative).
✅ "I can barely see anything." — This is correct.

❌ "There's no barely any time left." — Wrong.
✅ "There's barely any time left." — Correct.

This rule is the same for similar words like hardly and scarcely.

These words are very close in meaning to "barely" and can often replace it:

  • Hardly → "I hardly slept." (same meaning, slightly more formal)
  • Scarcely → "She could scarcely believe it." (same meaning, more literary/formal)
  • Only just → "I only just passed." (more casual, conversational)
  • Just → "I just managed to finish in time." (similar, but "just" is broader and used in many other ways too)

Of these, "hardly" and "barely" are the most interchangeable in everyday speech.

One sentence to remember it forever:

"Barely" means something did happen — but it was the closest thing to not happening.
